steps.title: Start here
steps.body: These numbers summarise everything happening on your network right now. Total traffic is how much has moved; active flows is how many conversations are currently open. Nothing here is a verdict yet -- it's just what NetAudit has actually observed.

steps.title: Encrypted vs plaintext
steps.body: This panel splits your traffic by whether it can be read in transit. Encrypted traffic (TLS/HTTPS) hides content but not metadata -- who you talked to and how much is still visible. Plaintext can be read in full by anyone on the path.

steps.title: The security score
steps.body: One number, A to F, built from your host posture, active threats, and hygiene recommendations. It's a starting point for 'how am I doing', not the whole picture -- the posture and threats views behind it are where the actual detail lives.

steps.title: What tier you're capturing on
steps.body: NetAudit degrades gracefully depending on what your machine allows: full packet capture with Npcap and admin rights, raw IPv4 headers with admin only, or connection-table sampling with neither. This banner tells you which one is active and what you're missing because of it -- worth reading before you trust an absence of findings as 'nothing's wrong'.

steps.title: Every observed conversation
steps.body: Every packet or flow NetAudit has seen, live and searchable: time, protocol, direction, peer, resolved hostname, owning process, bytes, and a risk indicator. This is the raw material everything else in the tool is built from.

steps.title: Filtering down to what matters
steps.body: With this much traffic, filtering is how you actually find anything. Try narrowing to one protocol or one process and see how the table updates instantly.

steps.title: Opening a row
steps.body: Click any row to open its full detail: every field NetAudit captured about that one conversation, not just what fits in the table.
steps.action_hint: click a row to open its detail drawer

steps.title: Active connections right now
steps.body: A live view of open connections, grouped by process -- what's talking to what, right now, rather than the traffic log's full history.

steps.title: Reading the risk column
steps.body: Each connection carries a rough risk indicator -- external vs local, plaintext vs encrypted, recognised port vs not. It's a prompt to look closer, not a verdict on its own; the explain endpoint behind any flagged item will tell you exactly why it's flagged.

steps.title: Hygiene recommendations
steps.body: Advice derived from what NetAudit actually observed on your network -- not a generic checklist. Each one explains what was seen, why it matters, and exactly what to do about it.

steps.title: The fix is yours to run
steps.body: NetAudit never runs a remediation command itself. Every fix here is copy-pasteable text you review and run yourself -- open one and see the exact command it suggests.
steps.action_hint: open one and copy its fix command

steps.title: Host security posture
steps.body: Around 40 read-only checks of how this machine itself is configured -- firewall, SMB, remote access, accounts, and more -- each reporting what was found, why it matters, and how to fix it.

steps.title: Browsing by category
steps.body: Checks are grouped into ten categories. A failing check here is a fact about this machine's configuration, not a behaviour observed on the wire -- that's what makes it different from a threat finding.

steps.title: Behavioural threat detection
steps.body: 22 detectors watching captured traffic for patterns associated with real attacker techniques -- beaconing, scanning, spoofing, lateral movement, and more -- each mapped to a MITRE ATT&CK technique where one genuinely fits.

steps.title: Reading a threat's reasoning
steps.body: Every threat shows its actual numbers, not just a label -- click one to see exactly what was measured and why it crossed the threshold, plus its documented false-positive causes, so you can judge it yourself rather than take the severity on faith.
steps.action_hint: click a threat to see its evidence and worked reasoning
